scenes.say: A product page takes two hundred milliseconds to load. By the end, you'll make it take two, and handle a payment message that arrives twice without charging twice.
Today you will do three things. Check Redis before the database. Keep cached data fresh. And survive a payment message that arrives twice.
lines: Charge once, even if delivered twice

scenes.title: Slow product page
scenes.statement: A product page reads the database on every view. Make repeat views fast without serving wrong data.
scenes.say: Here is the problem. A product page reads the database on every view. For example, two hundred milliseconds each time. We want about two on repeat views. Sixty seconds of staleness is fine.

scenes.head: One product page read
scenes.say: Here's why this matters. One product page reads from the database in two hundred milliseconds. Redis, which keeps data in memory, answers in about two. That's a hundred times faster, and every hit spares your database.

scenes.head: A cache is a sticky note
scenes.say: You need one phone number all day. The library across town has it, but the drive takes five minutes. A sticky note on your monitor has it in five seconds. So the cache is the sticky note, and the database is the library.

scenes.head: Cache-aside: check, miss, fill
scenes.say: The app asks Redis first. Redis is empty, so that's a miss. The app reads the database, which costs two hundred milliseconds. Then it saves a copy in Redis, with a sixty second T T L. The next request finds the copy: a hit, two milliseconds. This is cache-aside: the app manages the cache itself.

scenes.head: Cache-aside in code
scenes.say: In code, build a key, like product colon seven. Ask Redis. On a hit, return at once. On a miss, read the database, then save the price with set e x for sixty seconds. The loop calls it twice: a miss, then a hit.
Your turn. Same product, cold cache. Three requests arrive within ten seconds. How many of them read the database? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Cold cache, 3 requests in 10 s. Database reads?

scenes.head: Three requests, one database read
scenes.say: One. The first request misses and fills Redis. The second hits. So does the third. Two hundred milliseconds, then two, then two.

scenes.head: The catch: stale data
scenes.say: Now the catch. Someone changes the price in the database to ninety dollars. Redis still holds one hundred. The next user hits the cache and sees the old price. That's stale data. It lasts until the T T L expires, at most sixty seconds.

scenes.title: Stale sale price
scenes.statement: The price changed in the database, but the cache still holds the old one. Fix freshness, and survive a hot key expiring.
scenes.note: 1,000 requests when a hot key expires
scenes.say: New problem. The price changed in the database, but Redis still holds the old one. For example, ninety against one hundred. We want users to see ninety. And a hot key expiring must not flatten the database.

scenes.head: Two cures for stale data
scenes.say: Picture a sale that ends at midnight. Redis keeps showing the sale price all morning. Cure one: peel the sticky note off when the number changes. That's invalidation. Cure two: stamp every note with an expiry date. That's the T T L, your safety net if a peel is ever missed.

scenes.head: Invalidation in code
scenes.say: Here's invalidation. Write the new price to the database first. Then delete the cached key. We read before the change and get a hit with the old price. After set price, the next read misses, reloads, and shows ninety dollars.

panels.code:
def set_price(pid, price):
    db_write(pid, price)
    r.delete(f"product:{pid}")

print(*get_product(7))
set_price(7, "$90")
print(*get_product(7))

scenes.say: Your turn. A hot product's key expires at noon. Refilling takes two hundred milliseconds, and one thousand requests arrive in that window. How many reach the database? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Hot key expires; 1,000 requests in 200 ms. DB reads?

scenes.head: Cache stampede
scenes.say: About a thousand. Every request misses at the same moment, so every one runs the same query. That's a cache stampede, and the database Redis protected gets flattened. Fix one: let a single request refill while the rest wait. Fix two: add random jitter to each T T L, so keys don't all expire together.

scenes.head: More cache questions
scenes.say: Four quick ones. No T T L and no delete? Stale forever. If Redis goes down, fall back to the database. What to cache? Slow, popular, rarely changing data. Data that must be exact, read from the database.
rows: Stale forever. Always set a TTL

scenes.title: Checkout hangs
scenes.statement: Checkout sends an email and builds an invoice before replying, so the page hangs. Reply fast, do the work later.
scenes.say: New problem. Checkout waits for the email and the invoice before it replies. For example, the page just hangs. We want an instant reply, with the work done later. And noon spikes must not hurt.

scenes.head: A queue is a ticket rail
scenes.say: Picture checkout. You send an email and make an invoice, and the page hangs. A waiter pins a ticket on the rail and returns to the floor. Cooks take tickets at their own pace. The rail is the message queue.

scenes.head: Queue between API and workers
scenes.say: The API accepts the order, drops a job on the queue, and answers right away. A worker takes it and sends the email. A spike just makes the queue longer. Start more workers, and the backlog drains.

scenes.head: Respond now, work later
scenes.say: In code, a real broker, a separate service, holds the queue. This in-memory one stands in for it. Checkout puts the order on the queue and returns two oh two Accepted. The worker runs later and sends the email.

panels.code:
q = Queue()
def checkout(order):
    q.put(order)
    return "202 Accepted"
def worker():
    order = q.get()
    print("emailing", order)
print(checkout(42))
worker()

scenes.say: Your turn. Every worker crashes for an hour, and orders keep arriving. The queue is durable, so it stores jobs safely. What happens to the jobs? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: All workers down for an hour. What happens to jobs?

scenes.head: Workers down: jobs wait
scenes.say: They wait. The queue keeps every job while the workers are down. Six hundred pile up, and the API never slows. Workers return, and the backlog drains to zero. Nothing was lost. But a job can now run more than once.

scenes.title: Event delivered twice
scenes.statement: A payment_succeeded event can be delivered twice. Charge the customer exactly once.
scenes.note: the worker may crash before the ack
scenes.say: Last problem. A payment event can arrive twice. For example, event nine, delivered two times. We want one charge. And the worker may crash at any moment.

scenes.head: Where duplicates come from
scenes.say: Here's a favorite interview trap. The queue hands payment event nine to a worker. The worker charges the card. Then it crashes before sending the ack, the receipt that says done. No ack, so the queue assumes failure and delivers event nine again. That's at least once delivery: nothing is lost, but duplicates happen.

scenes.head: Idempotent consumer
scenes.say: The fix is an idempotent consumer: doing it twice equals doing it once. Every message carries a unique event id. Insert that id into a processed table, with the id as primary key. If the insert fails to add a row, we've seen it, so skip the charge. Only then ack. Event nine arrives twice, and charge prints once.

panels.code:
SQL = "INSERT INTO processed(id) VALUES (?) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING"
def handle(msg):
    with db:
        n = db.execute(SQL, (msg["id"],)).rowcount
        if n == 1:
            print("charge", msg["order"])
    ack(msg)
handle(evt)
handle(evt)

scenes.say: Your turn. Change handle to ack first, then do the work, and say the worker crashes right after the ack, before charging. What happens to event nine? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Ack first, crash before charging. Event nine is...

scenes.head: Ack first: the payment vanishes
scenes.say: Never charged. The ack told the queue the job was done, so it deleted event nine. The worker died before charging, so no retry ever comes. That's at most once delivery, and it loses payments. So ack after the work.

scenes.head: Delivery guarantees
scenes.say: At most once: ack first, and a crash loses the job. At least once: ack after the work, and a crash means a duplicate. Exactly once across systems is not possible. It's at least once, plus dedupe.
rows: metrics, where one loss is fine

scenes.head: Dedupe in three places
scenes.say: Three places to defend. Your own database: a processed table, in one transaction. An outside payment provider: send the event id as an idempotency key. A message that keeps failing: retry with growing waits, then park it in a dead letter queue.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: How does caching work? Check Redis, fill on a miss, set a T T L. Stale data? Delete the key on every update. Stampede? Let one request refill, and add random jitter.
rows: Cache-aside: check Redis, on a miss fill it, with a TTL
Delete the key on update; TTL is the safety net
One request refills; add TTL jitter

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Why a queue? The API answers fast, and workers do slow work later. Duplicates? Delivery is at least once, so dedupe on event id in a processed table. Exactly once? Not across systems. Ack after the work.
rows: Answer fast, work later, absorb spikes
At least once; dedupe on event id

scenes.head: Build these next
scenes.say: Three exercises. Cache your slowest endpoint for sixty seconds, and log hit or miss. Send one payment event twice and prove only one charge happens. Kill a worker mid job and watch the message come back.
So say this. Cache-aside: check Redis, fill it on a miss. Set a T T L, and delete on change. Queues deliver at least once, so dedupe on event id.
lines: Check Redis; on a miss, fill it.
Set a TTL; delete the key on change.
Queues deliver at least once: dedupe on id.
